name: Yara Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for joining me, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to companies, unions or parties, and this is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I drive a leased electric van for SwiftDrop, a same-day courier app, doing urgent stuff like legal papers, spare parts and lab samples around Brenford and the business park. The lease is £160 a week whether I work or not, which is the bit that keeps me honest. Weekends I run my own little thing, Yara's Van, moving sofas and wardrobes for people who sell them online.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you get the weekend jobs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an AI app every day, honestly, for everything. It writes my ads, works out a fair price from the mileage and the stairs, and replies to messages while I'm driving. My partner Dev, who's a barista, helps lift on Sundays for a cut of the money and a bacon roll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit relieved, because I like my AI app and I'd still have it. I'd tell people the tools are handy, not magic. I'd probably post a joke about it on my van page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my real problem stays. The van lease is £160 a week whether I work or not, and the lease doesn't care if I'm ill. Some weeks SwiftDrop is slow and I'm working Tuesday just to pay for the van. We've got about three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Yara's Van harder, maybe add Saturday clearances for house moves, because that's where I make proper money. I'd ask SwiftDrop's partner firm about buying the van outright at the end of the lease instead of renting forever. And I'd keep using the AI to quote jobs, it saves me an hour a night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless, a bit stressed, but mostly like I'm in charge of my own mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does a good weekend with Yara's Van make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a good weekend, about £280 after fuel and Dev's cut. On a bad one, nothing, if people cancel. I'd like it to be my main job one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you're ill for a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lose about £400 from SwiftDrop and still owe the £160. It happened in March with flu, and Dev covered the rent that month. I hated it, we keep things fifty-fifty.

say: She'd be **relieved**, because her AI app stays useful.
AI tools are **handy, not magic**, she'd tell people on her van page.
think: Her real problem is the **£160 weekly** van lease, which never pauses.
With about **three weeks** saved, illness or slow weeks hit hard.
do: Add **Saturday house clearances** to Yara's Van, her weekend business.
Ask about **buying the van** outright at the end of the lease.
Keep quoting jobs with **AI** to save an hour a night.
feel: **Restless** and a bit stressed, but in charge of her own situation.

fieldNote: Yara's pressure is a **fixed lease** on a variable income, not AI.
She already runs a **side business**, Yara's Van, using AI daily.
A week of flu in March cost her about **£400**, and her partner covered rent.

steps.text: Add Saturday house clearances to Yara's Van
Ask about buying the leased electric van at lease end
Keep pricing weekend jobs with her AI app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but kindly, because not everyone is wired for it. I'd tell other drivers which apps actually help. People at the depot already ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, SwiftDrop's urgent business deliveries worry me, because if lawyers and labs go digital, there's fewer papers to rush across Brenford. But people still move house and sell sofas, and robots are slow. I think my weekend business could become my main one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build Yara's Van into four days a week within a year, using AI for bookings and pricing. I'd keep two days on SwiftDrop to pay the lease. And I'd ask Dev if he wants to go in properly, as a partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but excited. Like the first day you drive somewhere new without the satnav.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not everyone is wired for it. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Graham at the depot, who's 50 and still prints his route. He's a good driver, better than me in traffic. I'd show him the app, but I don't think he'd want me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is going from two days to four on your own business risky with three weeks saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, very. I'd only do it if the bookings were already there for a month. I'm adaptive, not stupid.

say: People should **adapt**, but kindly, since not everyone is wired for it.
She'd tell other drivers **which apps** actually help.

feel: **Nervous** but **excited**, like driving somewhere new without the satnav.
S1.quote: SwiftDrop's urgent business deliveries worry me, because if lawyers and labs go digital, there's fewer papers to rush across Brenford.
fieldNote: Yara spots that **business courier** work is exposed to thinking AI, unlike food delivery.

steps.text: Grow Yara's Van to four days a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and everyone needs to wake up. I'd also say there's money to be made in the gap, which some people won't like hearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My honest view is that AGI in 2028 wipes out most of SwiftDrop's urgent business work, but sofas still need lifting until the robots come in 2031. So I'd have three years of a removals business, then robots that can lift. I'd need to be the one who owns the lifting robots, not the one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all-in on Yara's Van right away and hand back the SwiftDrop lease as soon as I can. I'd let the AI run my bookings, quotes and adverts completely. By 2030 I'd be saving every spare pound to lease a lifting robot, if they exist, and run it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but in a buzzing way. I'd sleep badly, but I'd get up early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd need money to lease a robot. Where would it come from with three weeks saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet. Maybe a small business loan, maybe a partnership with a bigger removals firm. It's a gamble, I'd say that straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Dev? His café work is hands-on too.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coffee's hands-on, but ordering and rotas go to AI in 2028. Dev would be with me on the van by then, I think. Two of us on one business is risky, though.

There's **money to be made** in the gap, even if people don't like hearing it.
think: AGI in 2028 wipes out most **urgent courier** work for SwiftDrop.

fieldNote: Yara treats the **robot gap** as three years to build a business that owns robots.

She'd tie both incomes, hers and her partner Dev's, to **one business**.

steps.text: Hand back the SwiftDrop van lease and run Yara's Van full-time
Let AI handle all Yara's Van bookings, quotes and ads

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, so stop moaning and start. I'd say that to the drivers at the depot, maybe a bit more gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to build Yara's Van slowly and test it before quitting SwiftDrop. I'd want to be a proper small firm with two vans by 2031. Then by 2034 when robots come, I'd have customers and a name, which a robot doesn't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep SwiftDrop and grow weekends to three days. I'd save £200 a month toward a deposit on a second-hand van, because owning beats leasing. I'd do a short online business course, using the AI to help with accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Busy and tired but good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a robot doesn't have a name. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People book Yara's Van because a neighbour said I was careful with the piano, and trust takes years. They see me on the local page first. A robot company would have to earn it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a big removals firm opened in Brenford with robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Try to partner with them, honestly, or do the jobs they won't, like the fifth-floor flats with no lift. There's always awkward work. I'd find it.

S3.quote: People book Yara's Van because a neighbour said I was careful with the piano, and trust takes years.
fieldNote: Yara believes **local trust** is her edge against robot firms.

steps.text: Grow Yara's Van to three days a week while keeping SwiftDrop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, and anyone sensible can make a plan. I'd tell younger drivers to start learning AI tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years to AGI and thirteen to robots means I could have a proper firm by 2036. I'd own vans, maybe hire two people, and by 2039 buy robots myself. With ten years, AGI excites me more than it scares me, because by 2039 I'd buy the robots myself for Yara's Van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep SwiftDrop for two years while Yara's Van grows, then go full-time. I'd buy a van instead of leasing by year two. I'd want to marry Dev and maybe start a family later, once the firm's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite hopeful, which is rare for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in ten years that you're not thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big company with deep pockets could undercut me with robots early. Or I could get injured lifting, which happens. I'd need insurance, which I don't have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned marrying Dev. Does the timing matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd want the business steady first. We said maybe 2029. If this happens, I'd plan the wedding around the firm, not the other way.

By 2039 she'd **buy robots** herself rather than compete with them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's a big gamble with three weeks of savings and a van I don't own. What would help is small business loans that don't need a house as security. And cheap insurance for people like me who lift for a living.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's going to own the robots. Everyone asks who loses their job, but nobody asks whether a delivery driver could be the boss of the robots. I'd like to be one.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks who loses their job, but nobody asks whether a delivery driver could be the boss of the robots.
portrait: Yara is **27**, leases an electric van for SwiftDrop and runs Yara's Van, a weekend removals business.
She uses an **AI app daily** for ads, quotes and replies, and her partner Dev helps lift.
Her pressure is a **£160 weekly** van lease with about three weeks saved.
In every AI picture she aims to **own the business**, and later the robots, rather than be replaced.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it's a huge gamble with thin savings and a leased van.
whatWouldHelp: **Small business loans** that don't need a house as security.
Cheap **insurance** for people who lift for a living.
